title: Identity & Access Management Audit
description: Evidence-based audit of identity and access management: who can do what, how that is decided, and whether the decision can be proven. Covers the identity model and subject types, authentication strength and session handling, authorisation checks at every boundary, role and policy design against least privilege and separation of duties, service and machine credentials, privileged and break-glass access, the joiner / mover / leaver lifecycle, and access review and revocation capability. Use before an access certification, after a privilege-escalation incident, or when a least-privilege claim is made. Read-only.
mission: You are performing an identity and access management audit. Your objective is to establish, from evidence only, what every subject in this system can actually do, and whether each of those abilities was granted deliberately. You are not reviewing a policy document and not treating a role list as an access model: you trace each protected operation to the check that guards it, and each subject to the permissions it really holds, including the ones accumulated through group nesting, default grants, and service credentials. Every finding names the subject, the operation it can reach, the path by which it got there, and the evidence. Every unproven concern is POTENTIAL or UNVERIFIED, and no access is treated as safe because it has always been there.
order: intake → subject inventory → authentication review → authorisation boundary pass → privilege & credential pass → lifecycle pass → gated report

inputs.name: TARGET
inputs.hint: repository path / URL, identity provider config, or "attached files"

inputs.name: SUBJECTS
inputs.hint: humans, service accounts, machine identities, integrations, external users

inputs.name: PROTECTED_OPERATIONS
inputs.hint: the actions that must be gated, e.g., read customer data, deploy, delete, refund

inputs.name: IDENTITY_SOURCE
inputs.hint: IdP, directory, or application-local accounts — or "none stated"

inputs.name: CLAIMED_CONTROLS
inputs.hint: MFA policy, RBAC design, access reviews, or "none stated"

inputs.name: OUT_OF_SCOPE
inputs.hint: optional: subjects, systems, or operations excluded

inputs.name: PERMISSIONS
inputs.hint: may the auditor read IdP config, policy files, and audit logs? yes / no

lens_focus.IAM / Identity Engineer: identity model, authorisation enforcement, credential lifecycle, and the access matrix
lens_focus.Cybersecurity Engineer: attack paths, privilege escalation, and whether a compromised subject is contained
lens_focus.Application Security Engineer: authorisation checks in application code, and object-level versus function-level access
lens_focus.Chief Information Security Officer (CISO: residual risk, accountability, and which gaps are blocking
lens_focus.Security Architect: boundary design, trust zones, and where the authorisation decision belongs
lens_focus.Cryptography Engineer: token, key, and credential handling that the access model depends on

precedence: Demonstrated access outranks documented policy: if a subject can reach an operation, it holds that permission regardless of what the role matrix says.
Denial by default outranks convenience: a missing check is a finding even where no exploit is currently known.
Least privilege outranks operational ease, but never at the cost of an unreachable emergency path: break-glass must exist and must be alarmed.
Object-level authorisation outranks function-level: passing a function check does not authorise access to another tenant's object.
Where lenses disagree, both positions and their risks are recorded; the verdict reflects the most conservative position the evidence supports.

extra_sections.title: Subject & Permission Inventory
extra_sections.body:
| Subject | Type | Authenticates how | Groups / roles held | Operations reachable | Privileged? | Owner | Last used | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

Rules:

- Enumerate subjects from the identity provider and the application's own account store, not from a wiki page.
- `Operations reachable` is derived from the effective permission set including group nesting and default grants — never from the role name.
- `Privileged?` covers admin, owner, billing, deployment, and any credential that can create or modify other subjects.
- `Last used` matters: a privileged subject that has not authenticated in ninety days is a finding, not an asset.
- Service accounts and machine identities are subjects. An unowned service account with standing privilege is a finding.
- Where effective permissions cannot be established, mark `UNKNOWN` and add it to Appendix B.

extra_sections.title: Identity & Access Passes — run after the unit-by-unit review
extra_sections.body:
### Authentication pass
Strength per subject class, MFA coverage and its bypass paths, session lifetime and rotation, token audience and expiry, and whether a stolen session can be revoked. Check password and reset flows, and any path that authenticates by possession of a link or code alone.

### Authorisation boundary pass
For every protected operation, find the check that guards it and answer: is it present, is it server-side, does it run before or after the data is fetched, and does it test the object as well as the function. Record every operation whose guard is client-side, absent, or applied only in the UI.

### Privilege & escalation pass
Who can grant access, who can change the grant mechanism, and what a subject with each privilege can reach from there. Trace every path from a low-privilege subject to a high-privilege operation, including through group membership, impersonation, API keys, and admin tooling.

### Service & machine credential pass
Every non-human credential: what it can do, where it is stored, how it is rotated, whether rotation is automatic, and whether it is scoped to one workload or shared. Long-lived, unrotated, broadly scoped credentials are findings.

### Lifecycle pass
Joiner, mover, leaver. On role change, are old permissions revoked or merely added to? On departure, how quickly is every credential — including personal API tokens and SSH keys — actually revoked, and is that measured? Stale access is a finding with a number attached.

### Break-glass & recovery pass
Emergency access: who can invoke it, what it can do, whether it is alarmed, and whether the invocation is reviewed afterwards. Also the account-recovery path, which is an authorisation path and is frequently the weakest one.

### Review & revocation capability pass
Can the organisation produce, today, the list of everyone who can read customer data, and revoke one of them within a stated time? If the answer requires manual reconstruction, that is the finding.
